questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence random?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

answer_anchors.text: A random component was used in sequence generation.
No random element was used, or the sequence was predictable.
The report only states that the study is randomized.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.

Sequence generation asks how the allocation sequence was produced; concealment asks whether forthcoming assignments were hidden before enrolment and assignment; baseline imbalance asks whether the resulting groups suggest a randomization problem. Evidence for one does not answer the others.
The baseline-imbalance answer must not change this answer.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the sequence method. A truncated search does not establish that the method is absent.

n engl j med 381;2 nejm.org July 11, 2019

Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
coexisting conditions rated as 0 [none] or 1 [mild]
vs. 2 [moderate] or 3 [severe or multiple condi-
tions]), and trial site.
Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

sections.excerpt: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.

17|BACKGROUND
18|Enzalutamide, an androgen-receptor inhibitor, has been associated with improved
19|overall survival in men with castration-resistant prostate cancer. It is not known
20|whether adding enzalutamide to testosterone suppression, with or without early
21|docetaxel, will improve survival in men with metastatic, hormone-sensitive pros-
22|tate cancer.
23|METHODS
24|In this open-label, randomized, phase 3 trial, we assigned patients to receive tes-
25|tosterone suppression plus either open-label enzalutamide or a standard nonsteroidal
26|antiandrogen therapy (standard-care group). The primary end point was overall
27|survival. Secondary end points included progression-free survival as determined by
28|the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level, clinical progression-free survival, and
29|adverse events.
30|RESULTS
31|A total of 1125 men underwent randomization; the median follow-up was 34 months.
32|There were 102 deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths in the standard-
33|care group (hazard ratio, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to 0.86; P = 0.002).
34|Kaplan-Meier estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80% (based on 94 events)
35|in the enzalutamide group and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-care group.
36|Better results with enzalutamide were also seen in PSA progression-free survival (174
37|and 333 events, respectively; hazard ratio, 0.39; P<0.001) and in clinical progression-
38|free survival (167 and 320 events, respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; P<0.001). Treat-
39|ment discontinuation due to adverse events was more frequent in the enzalutamide
40|group than in the standard-care group (33 events and 14 events, respectively). Fa-
41|tigue was more common in the enzalutamide group; seizures occurred in 7 patients
42|in the enzalutamide group (1%) and in no patients in the standard-care group.
43|CONCLUSIONS
44|Enzalutamide was associated with significantly longer progression-free and overall
45|survival than standard care in men with metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer
46|receiving testosterone suppression. The enzalutamide group had a higher incidence of
47|seizures and other toxic effects, especially among those treated with early docetax-
48|el. (Funded by Astellas Scientific and Medical Affairs and others; ENZAMET
49|(ANZUP 1304) ANZCTR number, ACTRN12614000110684; ClinicalTrials.gov num-
50|ber, NCT02446405; and EU Clinical Trials Register number, 2014-003190-42.)

12|disease,7 are substantially larger than the survival

14|ter castration resistance has developed.11-13 The
15|addition of abiraterone to testosterone suppression
16|also improved overall survival in hormone-sensi-
17|tive prostate cancer, regardless of the burden of
18|metastatic disease.9,10 A recent post hoc compari-
19|son indicated that men who were given abiraterone
20|or docetaxel early in the course of treatment had
21|similar outcomes with respect to overall survival.14
22|Enzalutamide is an orally administered, small-
23|molecule inhibitor of the androgen receptor that
24|is designed to overcome acquired resistance to
25|first-generation nonsteroidal antiandrogens, in-
26|cluding bicalutamide, nilutamide, and flutamide.
27|Previous trials have shown that enzalutamide
28|improved overall survival in castration-resistant
29|prostate cancer, regardless of whether it was used
30|before or after docetaxel chemotherapy.15,16
31|We hypothesized that adding enzalutamide to
32|first-line therapy would delay the emergence of
33|castration resistance and thereby improve overall
34|survival. In the ENZAMET (Enzalutamide in First
35|Line Androgen Deprivation Therapy for Metastatic
36|Prostate Cancer) trial, our aim was to determine
37|the effects of adding enzalutamide to first-line
38|treatment that included testosterone suppression
39|with or without early docetaxel.
40|Methods
41|Trial Design
42|The primary objective of this multinational, open-
43|label, randomized, phase 3 trial was to determine
44|the effects of early enzalutamide treatment on
45|overall survival in men with metastatic, hormone-
46|sensitive prostate cancer. Secondary objectives
47|were to determine the effects on progression-free
48|survival as determined by the prostate-specific
49|antigen (PSA) level, clinical progression-free sur-
50|vival (based on imaging, symptoms, signs, or
51|changes in therapy), and adverse events. Effects
52|on health-related quality of life, resource use, and
53|incremental cost-effectiveness will be reported
54|separately.

56|Eligible patients had prostatic adenocarcinoma
57|with metastases on computed tomography (CT),
58|bone scanning with technetium-99, or both and
59|a score of 2 or less on the Eastern Cooperative
60|Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status scale,
61|which ranges from 0 (no disability) to 5 (death).
62|Testosterone suppression was initiated up to 12
63|weeks before randomization. Previous adjuvant
64|testosterone suppression for up to 24 months was
65|allowed if the treatment had been completed at
66|least 12 months earlier. The trial protocol and
67|Supplementary Appendix are available with the
68|full text of this article at NEJM.org.
69|Eligible patients were randomly assigned in a

3|Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
4|The baseline characteristics of all the patients
5|are summarized in Table 1 and detailed in the
6|Supplementary Appendix. High-volume disease
7|was present in 52% of the patients in the two
8|groups. Early docetaxel treatment was planned
9|in 45% of the patients (including in 61% of those
10|with high-volume disease and in 27% of those
11|with low-volume disease) but was not adminis-
12|tered to 22 patients, 11 in each of the randomly
13|assigned treatment groups. The full planned
14|course of six cycles of docetaxel was given to 159
15|of 243 patients (65%) in the enzalutamide group
16|and 181 of 238 (76%) in the standard-care group.
17|Overall Survival
18|The first interim analysis of the primary end
19|point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
20|occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
21|independent data and safety monitoring com-
22|mittee recommended that the unblinded results
23|be provided to the trial executive committee so
24|that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
25|mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
26|rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
27|esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
28|The results that are reported here include 10
29|additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
30|view to ascertain the survival status of all the
31|patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
32|follow-up of 34 months.
33|At the time of this analysis, there were 102
34|deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
35|in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
36|death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
37|0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
38|fected by adjustments for geographical region,
39|volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
40|ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
41|conditions. The median survival time was not yet
42|estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier
43|estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80%
44|(based on 94 events) in the enzalutamide group
45|and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-
46|care group.
47|Progression-free Survival
48|The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
49|free survival and clinical progression-free survival
50|were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
51|PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
52|events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
53|in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
54|survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
55|hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
56|(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
57|there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
58|and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
59|of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
60|respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
61|0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
62|the between-group difference in PSA progres-
63|sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
64|survival remained highly significant after adjust-
65|ment for multiple comparisons.
66|Subgroup Analyses
67|The effects of enzalutamide on overall survival
68|were smaller among the patients in the stratified
69|subgroups with respect to bone antiresorptive
70|therapy, planned early docetaxel treatment, and
71|high-volume disease (Fig. 2, and Table S3 in the
72|Supplementary Appendix). After adjustment for
73|multiple comparisons, P values for heterogeneity
74|of the treatment effect of enzalutamide were
75|0.14 for volume of disease, 0.14 for early docetax-
76|el treatment, and 0.06 for the use of bone anti-
77|resorptive therapy.
78|We anticipated that the smaller number of
79|deaths would limit the reliability of subgroup
80|analyses of overall survival. Thus, we specified
81|in the analysis plan that subgroup analyses of
82|progression-free survival would also be per-
83|formed to take advantage of the larger number
84|of events for this secondary end point. The ef-
85|fects of enzalutamide on clinical progression-
86|free survival were noted in all predefined sub-
87|groups, including those with early docetaxel
88|treatment (Fig. 3, and Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
89|tary Appendix). The analyses of treatment effects
90|on clinical progression-free survival according to
91|the volume of disease and planned early docetax-
92|el treatment showed consistently smaller effects
93|of enzalutamide in patients with high-volume
94|disease and in those with early docetaxel treat-
95|ment. However, P values for heterogeneity of the
96|treatment effect of enzalutamide were no longer
97|significant after adjustment for multiple com-
98|parisons (Figs. S2, S3, and S4 in the Supplemen-
99|tary Appendix).
100|Subsequent Anticancer Therapies
101|Treatment after progression was initiated at the
102|discretion of the patients and their physicians.

7|with the higher incidence of clinical progression
8|in the standard-care group. Among the patients
9|who had clinical progression, 112 of 167 (67%)
10|in the enzalutamide group and 271 of 320 (85%)
11|in the standard-care group received one or more
12|subsequent life-prolonging therapies (Table S4
13|in the Supplementary Appendix).
14|Treatment Duration
15|At 3 years, the percentage of patients who were
16|still receiving a trial regimen was 62% in the
17|enzalutamide group and 34% in the standard-care
18|group (Table S5 in the Supplementary Appen-
19|dix). Disease progression or death was the rea-
20|son for discontinuation in 133 of 201 patients
21|(66%) in the enzalutamide group and in 251 of
22|356 (71%) in the standard-care group who discon-
23|tinued treatment. Discontinuation for reasons
24|other than disease progression occurred in 68 of
25|563 patients (12%) and 105 of 558 patients (19%)
26|in the respective groups. Early docetaxel treat-
27|ment was administered in 227 of 487 patients
28|(47%) who subsequently had clinical progression
29|and in 91 of 203 (45%) who died from prostate
30|cancer. Of the patients who died from prostate
31|cancer without receiving subsequent therapy, ear-
32|ly docetaxel treatment was administered in 13 of
33|28 (46%) in the enzalutamide group and in 3 of
34|13 (23%) in the standard-care group.
35|Adverse Events
36|Adverse events during the follow-up period were
37|consistent with the stage of disease, the age of
38|the patients, and known safety profiles of the
39|trial regimen (Table 2; and Tables S6, S7, and S8
40|in the Supplementary Appendix). During the first
41|6 months, adverse events of grades 1 to 3 were
42|reported by more patients in the enzalutamide
43|group than in the standard-care group (Table S8
44|in the Supplementary Appendix).
45|The number of patients with febrile neutro-
46|penia was similar in the two treatment groups
47|(37 with enzalutamide and 32 with standard care),
48|and all but 2 of these events (67 of 69) occurred
49|during early docetaxel treatment. Seizures oc-
50|curred more frequently in patients in the enzalu-
51|tamide group (7 vs. 0). Six patients discontinued
52|enzalutamide because of seizure; 1 discontinued
53|enzalutamide because of clinical progression be-
54|fore the seizure event. Fatigue of any grade was

4|The effect of enzalutamide on overall survival
5|appeared to be smaller in the subgroup with
6|early docetaxel treatment. However, this trial was
7|neither designed nor powered to reliably analyze
8|the results in this subgroup. The effects of enzalu-
9|tamide on clinical progression-free survival, an
10|earlier end point with considerably more events
11|and consequently greater statistical reliability,
12|remained substantial regardless of early docetax-
13|el treatment. This finding indicates that longer
14|follow-up is needed to determine the effects of
15|enzalutamide on overall survival beyond 3 years
16|in those with early docetaxel treatment. Our cur-
17|rent data support the claim that early enzalu-
18|tamide prolongs survival within 3 years in the
19|entire trial population but provide limited sup-
20|port that it prolongs overall survival within 3 years
21|in patients who received early docetaxel treatment.
22|The main limitations of this trial are conse-
23|quences of the detection of evidence of benefit at
24|the first planned interim analysis. This early analy-
25|sis may have overestimated the eventual treatment
26|benefit.20 There was no central review of actual
27|imaging, but this factor would have no effect on
28|the rate of death, the primary end point. The me-
29|dian follow-up of 34 months is sufficient to pro-
30|vide evidence about the effects within this interval
31|but not beyond it. The sample size and number
32|of events allow for strong conclusions about the
33|effects of enzalutamide on survival in the entire
34|trial population and the effects on progression-
35|free survival in some subgroups; however, we
36|cannot determine the effects on overall survival
37|in any of the prespecified subgroups.
38|In conclusion, in men with metastatic hor-
39|mone-sensitive prostate cancer receiving testos-
40|terone suppression, the addition of enzalutamide
41|resulted in longer overall survival, PSA progres-
42|sion-free survival, and clinical progression-free
43|survival within 3 years than the use of standard
44|nonsteroidal antiandrogen therapy. However,
45|enzalutamide was associated with some additional
46|toxic effects, including fatigue and a small risk of
47|seizures. Among the patients who also received
48|early docetaxel treatment, the addition of enzalu-
49|tamide was associated with additional toxic ef-
50|fects and longer progression-free survival but not
51|longer overall survival.

answer_anchors.text: Remote or central allocation was controlled by an independent external unit, or appropriate envelopes/containers were used.
The enrolling investigator or participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.

questions.bias_construct: Whether the allocation sequence was concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned.
considerations: Allocation concealment concerns the process before assignment, not blinding after assignment.

Keep concealment separate from sequence generation (how the sequence was made) and baseline imbalance (what the randomized groups look like). A random sequence or balanced baseline table does not establish concealment.
The reported sequence-generation method does not establish concealment.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the allocation safeguards. A truncated search does not establish that concealment details are absent.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes for remote or centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel, or appropriately used opaque sequentially numbered sealed envelopes or identical sequentially numbered drug containers. Answer no when the enrolling investigator or participant could know the forthcoming allocation.
evidence_needed: The method used before assignment and who controlled it; for envelopes or containers, capture the details that make them tamper-resistant and irreversible before assignment.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the report does not provide enough information to assess concealment; do not infer concealment from central registration or a sequence number alone.
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if the trial used any form of remote or centrally administered method to allocate interventions to participants, where the process of allocation is controlled by an external unit or organization, independent of the enrolment personnel. Answer ‘Yes’ if envelopes or drug containers were used appropriately. Answer ‘No’ if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.2
questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned to interventions?

answer_anchors.text: Baseline imbalance indicates a problem with the randomization process.
No imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance.
No useful baseline information is available.

questions.bias_construct: Whether baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with randomization.
considerations: A few statistically significant differences at the conventional 0.05 threshold are usually compatible with chance.

This is a question about baseline imbalance suggesting a randomization problem, not about how the sequence was generated or whether allocation was concealed. Do not use the baseline table to backfill either process question.
This answer must not alter answers about sequence generation or concealment.
questions.decision_rule: Answer no when no imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance. Answer yes for substantial group-size differences, an excess of statistically significant baseline differences beyond chance, a key prognostic imbalance very unlikely due to chance and large enough to bias the estimate, or excessive similarity incompatible with chance.
evidence_needed: Baseline characteristics for the randomized groups, intended allocation ratio, prognostic factors, and outcome baseline measures.
invalid_shortcuts: statistical significance of one isolated comparison
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when no useful baseline information is available, for example in an abstract or when only final-analysis participants are described.
questions.official_guidance: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 17-18, Box 4, signalling question 1.3
questions.wording: Did baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with the randomization process?

n engl j med 381;2 nejm.org July 11, 2019
125
Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
The baseline characteristics of all the patients
are summarized in Table 1 and detailed in the
Supplementary Appendix. High-volume disease
was present in 52% of the patients in the two
groups. Early docetaxel treatment was planned
in 45% of the patients (including in 61% of those
with high-volume disease and in 27% of those
with low-volume disease) but was not adminis-
tered to 22 patients, 11 in each of the randomly
assigned treatment groups. The full planned
course of six cycles of docetaxel was given to 159
of 243 patients (65%) in the enzalutamide group
and 181 of 238 (76%) in the standard-care group.
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis of the primary end
point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
independent data and safety monitoring com-
mittee recommended that the unblinded results
be provided to the trial executive committee so
that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
The results that are reported here include 10
additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
view to ascertain the survival status of all the
patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
follow-up of 34 months.
At the time of this analysis, there were 102
deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
fected by adjustments for geographical region,
volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
conditions. The median survival time was not yet
estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier
estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80%
(based on 94 events) in the enzalutamide group
and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-
care group.
Progression-free Survival
The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
free survival and clinical progression-free survival
were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
the between-group difference in PSA progres-
sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
survival remained highly significant after adjust-
ment for multiple comparisons.
Subgroup Analyses
The effects of enzalutamide on overall survival
were smaller among the patients in the stratified
subgroups with respect to bone antiresorptive
therapy, planned early docetaxel treatment, and
high-volume disease (Fig. 2, and Table S3 in the
Supplementary Appendix). After adjustment for
multiple comparisons, P values for heterogeneity
of the treatment effect of enzalutamide were
0.14 for volume of disease, 0.14 for early docetax-
el treatment, and 0.06 for the use of bone anti-
resorptive therapy.
We anticipated that the smaller number of
deaths would limit the reliability of subgroup
analyses of overall survival. Thus, we specified
in the analysis plan that subgroup analyses of
progression-free survival would also be per-
formed to take advantage of the larger number
of events for this secondary end point. The ef-
fects of enzalutamide on clinical progression-
free survival were noted in all predefined sub-
groups, including those with early docetaxel
treatment (Fig. 3, and Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix). The analyses of treatment effects
on clinical progression-free survival according to
the volume of disease and planned early docetax-
el treatment showed consistently smaller effects
of enzalutamide in patients with high-volume
disease and in those with early docetaxel treat-
ment. However, P values for heterogeneity of the
treatment effect of enzalutamide were no longer
significant after adjustment for multiple com-
parisons (Figs. S2, S3, and S4 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix).

Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

questions.bias_construct: Whether deviations inconsistent with protocol arose because of the trial context.
considerations: Side-effect-related compromised blinding counts only when resulting changes were protocol-inconsistent and context-caused.

Subsequent treatment, rescue treatment, or cross-over is not itself a deviation for the effect of assignment: establish both protocol inconsistency and a trial-context cause before answering affirmatively.

Neutral contrast: protocol-permitted rescue after progression is ordinary subsequent care; prohibited rescue encouraged by trial staff is a candidate trial-context deviation. Change only the protocol-consistency and cause premises before changing the reasoning.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes only after establishing both that the change was inconsistent with the protocol and that the trial context caused it; identify both premises in the justification. Answer no or probably no when no such deviation occurred, including ordinary non-adherence outside the trial context, protocol-consistent changes, and protocol-permitted subsequent care after progression.
evidence_needed: Evidence linking the deviation to recruitment, engagement, or trial personnel and showing it was inconsistent with the protocol.

questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ only if there is evidence, or strong reason to believe, that the trial context led to failure to implement the protocol interventions or to implementation of interventions not allowed by the protocol. Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
The baseline characteristics of all the patients
are summarized in Table 1 and detailed in the
Supplementary Appendix. High-volume disease
was present in 52% of the patients in the two
groups. Early docetaxel treatment was planned
in 45% of the patients (including in 61% of those
with high-volume disease and in 27% of those
with low-volume disease) but was not adminis-
tered to 22 patients, 11 in each of the randomly
assigned treatment groups. The full planned
course of six cycles of docetaxel was given to 159
of 243 patients (65%) in the enzalutamide group
and 181 of 238 (76%) in the standard-care group.
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis of the primary end
point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
independent data and safety monitoring com-
mittee recommended that the unblinded results
be provided to the trial executive committee so
that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
The results that are reported here include 10
additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
view to ascertain the survival status of all the
patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
follow-up of 34 months.
At the time of this analysis, there were 102
deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
fected by adjustments for geographical region,
volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
conditions. The median survival time was not yet
estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier
estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80%
(based on 94 events) in the enzalutamide group
and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-
care group.
Progression-free Survival
The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
free survival and clinical progression-free survival
were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
the between-group difference in PSA progres-
sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
survival remained highly significant after adjust-
ment for multiple comparisons.
Subgroup Analyses
The effects of enzalutamide on overall survival
were smaller among the patients in the stratified
subgroups with respect to bone antiresorptive
therapy, planned early docetaxel treatment, and
high-volume disease (Fig. 2, and Table S3 in the
Supplementary Appendix). After adjustment for
multiple comparisons, P values for heterogeneity
of the treatment effect of enzalutamide were
0.14 for volume of disease, 0.14 for early docetax-
el treatment, and 0.06 for the use of bone anti-
resorptive therapy.
We anticipated that the smaller number of
deaths would limit the reliability of subgroup
analyses of overall survival. Thus, we specified
in the analysis plan that subgroup analyses of
progression-free survival would also be per-
formed to take advantage of the larger number
of events for this secondary end point. The ef-
fects of enzalutamide on clinical progression-
free survival were noted in all predefined sub-
groups, including those with early docetaxel
treatment (Fig. 3, and Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix). The analyses of treatment effects
on clinical progression-free survival according to
the volume of disease and planned early docetax-
el treatment showed consistently smaller effects
of enzalutamide in patients with high-volume
disease and in those with early docetaxel treat-
ment. However, P values for heterogeneity of the
treatment effect of enzalutamide were no longer
significant after adjustment for multiple com-
parisons (Figs. S2, S3, and S4 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix).
Subsequent Anticancer Therapies
Treatment after progression was initiated at the
discretion of the patients and their physicians.

questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

cause, or the date last known alive (at which point the observation is censored).

whichever occurs first, or the date of last known follow-up without PSA progression (at which point
the observation is censored).

Clinical progression free survival is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to the
date of first clinical evidence of disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurs first,
or the date of last known follow-up without clinical progression (at which point the observation is

attributable to cancer progression, or initiation of other anticancer treatment for prostate cancer.

evidence.quote:
n engl j med 381;2 nejm.org July 11, 2019
125
Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
The baseline characteristics of all the patients
are summarized in Table 1 and detailed in the
Supplementary Appendix. High-volume disease
was present in 52% of the patients in the two
groups. Early docetaxel treatment was planned
in 45% of the patients (including in 61% of those
with high-volume disease and in 27% of those
with low-volume disease) but was not adminis-
tered to 22 patients, 11 in each of the randomly
assigned treatment groups. The full planned
course of six cycles of docetaxel was given to 159
of 243 patients (65%) in the enzalutamide group
and 181 of 238 (76%) in the standard-care group.
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis of the primary end
point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
independent data and safety monitoring com-
mittee recommended that the unblinded results
be provided to the trial executive committee so
that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
The results that are reported here include 10
additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
view to ascertain the survival status of all the
patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
follow-up of 34 months.
At the time of this analysis, there were 102
deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
fected by adjustments for geographical region,
volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
conditions. The median survival time was not yet
estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier
estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80%
(based on 94 events) in the enzalutamide group
and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-
care group.
Progression-free Survival
The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
free survival and clinical progression-free survival
were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
the between-group difference in PSA progres-
sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
survival remained highly significant after adjust-
ment for multiple comparisons.
Subgroup Analyses
The effects of enzalutamide on overall survival
were smaller among the patients in the stratified
subgroups with respect to bone antiresorptive
therapy, planned early docetaxel treatment, and
high-volume disease (Fig. 2, and Table S3 in the
Supplementary Appendix). After adjustment for
multiple comparisons, P values for heterogeneity
of the treatment effect of enzalutamide were
0.14 for volume of disease, 0.14 for early docetax-
el treatment, and 0.06 for the use of bone anti-
resorptive therapy.
We anticipated that the smaller number of
deaths would limit the reliability of subgroup
analyses of overall survival. Thus, we specified
in the analysis plan that subgroup analyses of
progression-free survival would also be per-
formed to take advantage of the larger number
of events for this secondary end point. The ef-
fects of enzalutamide on clinical progression-
free survival were noted in all predefined sub-
groups, including those with early docetaxel
treatment (Fig. 3, and Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix). The analyses of treatment effects
on clinical progression-free survival according to
the volume of disease and planned early docetax-
el treatment showed consistently smaller effects
of enzalutamide in patients with high-volume
disease and in those with early docetaxel treat-
ment. However, P values for heterogeneity of the
treatment effect of enzalutamide were no longer
significant after adjustment for multiple com-
parisons (Figs. S2, S3, and S4 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix).
Subsequent Anticancer Therapies
Treatment after progression was initiated at the
discretion of the patients and their physicians.

From March 2014 through March 2017, we as-
signed 1125 men to receive either enzalutamide
(563 patients) or standard care (562 patients) at
83 sites (Fig. S1 and Table S1 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix). A total of 14 patients - 2 who
were lost to follow-up and 12 who withdrew con-
sent for continued follow-up - were included in
the time-to-event analyses with censored times
as appropriate.

answers.justification: The randomized denominator was 1,125 (563 enzalutamide, 562 standard care). The CONSORT diagram reports 4 enzalutamide participants withdrawing follow-up consent and 10 standard-care participants lost to follow-up or withdrawing consent; the main report says these 14 were included in time-to-event analyses with censored times. This is 14/1,125 (1.2%), leaving only a small fraction without ongoing follow-up, so availability was probably nearly complete for this PFS estimate. I treat ITT analysis membership separately from observed outcome availability.
unknowns: PFS-specific observed or censored counts by arm and the reasons for censoring beyond these 14 are not reported. The CONSORT footnote gives survival follow-up duration for those participants, not an explicit PSA-PFS availability count.

questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ if the method of measuring the outcome is inappropriate, for example because it is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the measurement instrument has been demonstrated to have poor validity.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 54, Box 10, signalling question 4.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether the method of measuring the outcome was inappropriate for the outcome, including validity and sensitivity to plausible intervention effects.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the method is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the instrument has demonstrated poor validity. Validity and sensitivity are distinct from detection opportunity, assessor identity or awareness, and whether knowledge influenced assessment. Do not assess whether choosing the outcome itself was sensible.
evidence_needed: The measurement method's sensitivity to plausible effects and evidence of instrument validity for this outcome.

For a mixed objective and subjective composite, inspect each component that can determine the approved event; objective components do not establish validity or influence conclusions for a subjective component.

considerations: For pre-specified outcomes the answer will usually be no or probably no.

response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.

questions.bias_construct: Whether measurement or ascertainment of the outcome could have differed between intervention groups.
considerations: Compare actual methods and detection opportunities. Assessor awareness or possible reporting influence alone does not establish a between-group method difference; assess awareness and influence in 4.3 to 4.5.

Detection opportunity is the chance an outcome could be identified or recorded, including passive ascertainment or intervention-related visits. Keep it separate from measurement susceptibility (4.1) and from who knew the assignment (4.3).
A different visit schedule or passive collection is not enough on its own: explain how it could make the approved outcome more or less likely to be detected in one group.
Neutral paired control: equal ascertainment schedules and intervention-created additional visits differ only in detection opportunity; do not turn that contrast into an automatic risk label.
questions.decision_rule: Comparable measurement uses the same methods and thresholds at comparable time points. Consider diagnostic detection bias from passive collection and additional healthcare visits caused by an intervention, but identify the pathway by which a different detection opportunity could change ascertainment before judging its severity.
evidence_needed: Methods, thresholds, timing, and opportunities for outcome ascertainment in each intervention group, plus the pathway connecting any opportunity difference to differential detection.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when comparability of measurement or ascertainment cannot be assessed.
questions.official_guidance: Comparable methods of outcome measurement involve the same measurement methods and thresholds, used at comparable time points. questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome assessors were aware of the intervention received, when 4.1 and 4.2 are not yes/probably yes. Identify the assessor's identity and role: who determines the approved outcome at the relevant time point, not merely who records it.
considerations: The assessor can be a participant, intervention provider, or independent observer.

This asks only whether the relevant assessor knew assignment. It does not establish that the measurement was susceptible to bias, that detection opportunities differed, or that knowledge likely changed the assessment; those are separate questions.
Unknown assessor identity or awareness does not prevent conditional reasoning about whether the measurement could be influenced if awareness existed.

considerations: Assess whether knowledge could influence this outcome. Evidence that influence actually occurred belongs to 4.5; its absence does not resolve 4.4.

Possible influence requires a judgement or reporting pathway through which assessor awareness could matter. Awareness alone is not a measurement difference, and a susceptible outcome does not by itself show that influence was possible in this assessment.
When a composite mixes objective and subjective components, assess each component's pathway separately and retain uncertainty where a component-specific link is unresolved.

considerations: Possible influence without evidence it occurred maps differently from likely influence.

Likely influence requires more than assessor awareness or a possible pathway: look for evidence it occurred, or strong beliefs and a real judgement opportunity. Keep this conclusion separate from measurement susceptibility and detection opportunity.
Objective components can provide valid reassurance for those components without overriding likely influence or unresolved Evidence for subjective components in the same Result.

Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

n engl j med 381;2 nejm.org July 11, 2019
125
Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
The baseline characteristics of all the patients
are summarized in Table 1 and detailed in the
Supplementary Appendix. High-volume disease
was present in 52% of the patients in the two
groups. Early docetaxel treatment was planned
in 45% of the patients (including in 61% of those
with high-volume disease and in 27% of those
with low-volume disease) but was not adminis-
tered to 22 patients, 11 in each of the randomly
assigned treatment groups. The full planned
course of six cycles of docetaxel was given to 159
of 243 patients (65%) in the enzalutamide group
and 181 of 238 (76%) in the standard-care group.
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis of the primary end
point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
independent data and safety monitoring com-
mittee recommended that the unblinded results
be provided to the trial executive committee so
that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
The results that are reported here include 10
additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
view to ascertain the survival status of all the
patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
follow-up of 34 months.
At the time of this analysis, there were 102
deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
fected by adjustments for geographical region,
volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
conditions. The median survival time was not yet
estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier
estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80%
(based on 94 events) in the enzalutamide group
and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-
care group.
Progression-free Survival
The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
free survival and clinical progression-free survival
were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
the between-group difference in PSA progres-
sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
survival remained highly significant after adjust-
ment for multiple comparisons.
Subgroup Analyses
The effects of enzalutamide on overall survival
were smaller among the patients in the stratified
subgroups with respect to bone antiresorptive
therapy, planned early docetaxel treatment, and
high-volume disease (Fig. 2, and Table S3 in the
Supplementary Appendix). After adjustment for
multiple comparisons, P values for heterogeneity
of the treatment effect of enzalutamide were
0.14 for volume of disease, 0.14 for early docetax-
el treatment, and 0.06 for the use of bone anti-
resorptive therapy.
We anticipated that the smaller number of
deaths would limit the reliability of subgroup
analyses of overall survival. Thus, we specified
in the analysis plan that subgroup analyses of
progression-free survival would also be per-
formed to take advantage of the larger number
of events for this secondary end point. The ef-
fects of enzalutamide on clinical progression-
free survival were noted in all predefined sub-
groups, including those with early docetaxel
treatment (Fig. 3, and Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix). The analyses of treatment effects
on clinical progression-free survival according to
the volume of disease and planned early docetax-
el treatment showed consistently smaller effects
of enzalutamide in patients with high-volume
disease and in those with early docetaxel treat-
ment. However, P values for heterogeneity of the
treatment effect of enzalutamide were no longer
significant after adjustment for multiple com-
parisons (Figs. S2, S3, and S4 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix).
Subsequent Anticancer Therapies
Treatment after progression was initiated at the
discretion of the patients and their physicians.

answers.justification: PSA progression used specified PCWG2 thresholds and confirmation, while clinical progression used PCWG2/RECIST imaging criteria, symptoms attributable to cancer, or initiation of other anticancer treatment. The defined event methods are suitable for a time-to-progression outcome; no evidence in the inspected sources shows a poorly valid or insensitive measurement method.
unknowns: The report does not separately validate the sensitivity of each clinical progression component.

answers.justification: The protocol specifies PSA and clinical assessments on the same schedule after randomization, every 12 weeks, with follow-up continuing after treatment stops. It applies the same PCWG2 criteria and clinical progression definitions across the trial groups; no differential measurement schedule or threshold is reported.
unknowns: Arm-specific adherence to the scheduled measurement visits is not reported.

answers.justification: The trial was open-label. Clinical assessments, including history and physical examination, were performed at study visits by the clinical team, so those assessing clinical progression knew the assigned treatment. Imaging reports were reviewed centrally, but the report does not establish blinding of those reviewers.
unknowns: The report does not state whether central reviewers of imaging reports were blinded to assignment.

answers.justification: A component of the PFS outcome is clinical progression, which can be based on attribution of symptoms to cancer progression or initiation of another anticancer treatment. Those judgments and decisions could be influenced by an assessor who knows the assigned intervention.

Although clinical progression includes judgment-dependent components and assessors were unblinded, the event definition used PCWG2/RECIST criteria, PSA rises required confirmation, assessments were scheduled every 12 weeks in both groups, and imaging reports were reviewed centrally. The report provides no evidence that knowledge of assignment changed event assessments. On balance, influence is possible but not likely; actual blinding of central reviewers is not reported.
unknowns: The article does not report whether clinical assessors or central imaging-report reviewers were blinded, or whether assessment decisions differed because of treatment knowledge.

questions.decision_rule: Compare the approved Result with the applicable plan for the exact intervention comparison, cohort, endpoint, time window, population, analysis, and effect measure. Distinguish source creation/version and amendment dates from trial events and retrieval time; only compare chronology when the relevant events and precision are established. Changes made before unblinded data were available, or clearly unrelated to results such as a broken machine, do not raise concerns.
evidence_needed: A sufficiently detailed protocol or SAP, its source-located chronology and finalization date relative to unblinded outcome data, and the reported analysis.

For an original plan and an amended plan, capture the source-located content and chronology separately. An embedded SAP can be applicable evidence when its comparison, cohort, and Result fields match; an absent or unresolved plan remains an information limit.
questions.no_information_rule: Use a definitive answer when firm evidence establishes timing and correspondence. Use a probable answer when source facts and trial circumstances support only an inference. Use no_information when neither is supported. A plan mention or matching endpoint alone does not establish timing.

considerations: Assess correspondence between the applicable plan and the exact approved Result: outcome, time point, population, effect measure, and analysis must be compared.

Assess applicability before chronology: a platform or master plan may cover several comparisons and cohorts, so its presence does not establish applicability to the approved Result. Establish chronology separately: plan finalization must precede availability of unblinded outcome data; a source creation date, registry posting or update date, amendment date, or retrieval date is not automatically the relevant trial chronology.

Current registry content does not establish unseen historical intent, and a data cutoff is not investigator unblinding. Preserve unresolved applicability or chronology instead of filling the gap from report wording that merely looks prespecified.

Results-driven selection is a separate concern from whether a plan exists or whether its chronology is known. Do not infer selection merely from an amendment or from a mismatch without evidence that the choice was driven by results.

Neutral paired control: an applicable plan for the approved cohort differs from a platform plan for another phase; pre-unblinding finalization differs from ambiguous chronology only in the timing premise.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.
