Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

n engl j med 381;2 nejm.org July 11, 2019
125
Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
The baseline characteristics of all the patients
are summarized in Table 1 and detailed in the
Supplementary Appendix. High-volume disease
was present in 52% of the patients in the two
groups. Early docetaxel treatment was planned
in 45% of the patients (including in 61% of those
with high-volume disease and in 27% of those
with low-volume disease) but was not adminis-
tered to 22 patients, 11 in each of the randomly
assigned treatment groups. The full planned
course of six cycles of docetaxel was given to 159
of 243 patients (65%) in the enzalutamide group
and 181 of 238 (76%) in the standard-care group.
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis of the primary end
point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
independent data and safety monitoring com-
mittee recommended that the unblinded results
be provided to the trial executive committee so
that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
The results that are reported here include 10
additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
view to ascertain the survival status of all the
patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
follow-up of 34 months.
At the time of this analysis, there were 102
deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
fected by adjustments for geographical region,
volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
conditions. The median survival time was not yet
estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier
estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80%
(based on 94 events) in the enzalutamide group
and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-
care group.
Progression-free Survival
The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
free survival and clinical progression-free survival
were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
the between-group difference in PSA progres-
sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
survival remained highly significant after adjust-
ment for multiple comparisons.
Subgroup Analyses
The effects of enzalutamide on overall survival
were smaller among the patients in the stratified
subgroups with respect to bone antiresorptive
therapy, planned early docetaxel treatment, and
high-volume disease (Fig. 2, and Table S3 in the
Supplementary Appendix). After adjustment for
multiple comparisons, P values for heterogeneity
of the treatment effect of enzalutamide were
0.14 for volume of disease, 0.14 for early docetax-
el treatment, and 0.06 for the use of bone anti-
resorptive therapy.
We anticipated that the smaller number of
deaths would limit the reliability of subgroup
analyses of overall survival. Thus, we specified
in the analysis plan that subgroup analyses of
progression-free survival would also be per-
formed to take advantage of the larger number
of events for this secondary end point. The ef-
fects of enzalutamide on clinical progression-
free survival were noted in all predefined sub-
groups, including those with early docetaxel
treatment (Fig. 3, and Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix). The analyses of treatment effects
on clinical progression-free survival according to
the volume of disease and planned early docetax-
el treatment showed consistently smaller effects
of enzalutamide in patients with high-volume
disease and in those with early docetaxel treat-
ment. However, P values for heterogeneity of the
treatment effect of enzalutamide were no longer
significant after adjustment for multiple com-
parisons (Figs. S2, S3, and S4 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix).
Subsequent Anticancer Therapies
Treatment after progression was initiated at the
discretion of the patients and their physicians.

7|Overall Survival (OS) (Primary Endpoint)
8|Overall survival is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to date of death from any
9|cause, or the date last known alive (at which point the observation is censored).
10|2.2
11|PSA Progression Free Survival (PSA PFS)
12|PSA progression free survival (PSA PFS) is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to
13|the date of first evidence of PSA progression, clinical progression, or death from any cause,
14|whichever occurs first, or the date of last PSA test without PSA progression (at which point the
15|observation is censored).
16|2.3
17|Clinical Progression Free Survival (Clinical PFS)
18|Clinical progression free survival is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to the
19|date of first clinical evidence of disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurs first,
20|or the date of last known follow-up without clinical progression (at which point the observation is
21|censored). The censoring date will be the latest of the following: the date of the patient's last
22|assessment during the 'on treatment' phase where clinical progression status is recorded as 'no';
23|and, the maximum date the patient is last known not to have progressed collected during the 'post-
24|treatment follow-up' phase. Clinical progression is defined by progression on imaging, development
25|of symptoms attributable to cancer progression, or initiation of other anticancer treatment for
26|prostate cancer.
27|2.4
28|Safety
29|The NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events Version 4.03 (NCI CTCAE) will be used to
30|classify and grade the intensity of adverse events whilst on treatment, at progression, and 30-42
31|days after the last dose of study treatment.
32|2.5
33|Quality of Life (QoL)
34|The core EORTC QoL Questionnaire (QLQ-C30) will be used in conjunction with the disease specific
35|module for prostate cancer (PR25). The EQ-5D will be used to obtain utility valuations on the health
36|states experienced by participants. All instruments will be scored according to standard conventions
37|(see Section 10.1 and 10.2).
38|2.6
39|Health Care Resource Usage
40|Information on the following areas of health-care resource usage will be collected: protocol therapy
41|and hospitalisations (for all participants by trial staff via standard case record forms (CRFs), visits to
42|health professionals (for Australian participants via Medicare benefits scheme (MBS) and for other
43|regions as specified separately in their Group Specific Appendix (GSA), and non-protocol medications
44|(for Australian participants via Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) and for other regions as
45|separately specified in their GSA).
46|3 Analysis Sets
47|All randomised participants will be eligible for inclusion in the full analysis set in accordance with the
48|intention-to-treat analysis principle. The full analysis set thus comprises the intention-to-treat (ITT)
49|population. The per-protocol population will comprise all randomised participants that are deemed
50|eligible/evaluable on blinded central clinical review. Patients are classified according to study

1|
2|Page 6
3|
4|medication assigned at the time of randomisation. The safety population will comprise all
5|randomised participants who received at least one administration of study medication.
6|If a patient receives at least one dose of enzalutamide (irrespective of randomised allocation) in the
7|period between randomisation and cessation of study treatment, they will be included in the
8|enzalutamide arm of the safety population. If that condition does not apply, and the patient receives
9|a least one dose of NSAA (irrespective of randomised allocation) in the period between
10|randomisation and cessation of study treatment, they will be included in the NSAA arm of the safety
11|population. If neither of the above criteria apply, the patient will be excluded from the safety
12|population.
13|
14|The reasons for any exclusions from analysis sets will be reviewed and endorsed by the Trial
15|Executive Committee and documented in the final study report.
16|
17|The primary analysis population used for the evaluation of enzalutamide on non-safety parameters
18|will be the ITT population. The per-protocol population may be used in secondary analyses of non-
19|safety parameters as part of a sensitivity analysis. Safety analyses will be performed using the safety
20|population.
21|4 Interim and Final Analyses
22|Assuming the study is not terminated early, the final analysis is planned to be undertaken after the
23|required number of deaths have occurred (i.e. N=470, see sample size section of the protocol). The
24|study design incorporates formal interim analyses performed on OS once 50%, 67%, and 80% of the
25|required events are observed. The interim analysis allows for early rejection of the null hypothesis
26|according to an alpha spending function with an O'Brien-Fleming boundary shape1. Indicative
27|boundaries for these analyses are presented in the table below. The actual number of events
28|observed at the time of the interim analyses would be used to construct the definitive rejection
29|boundary. The conditional power (CP) of the study will also be calculated for OS at the interim
30|analyses.2 This procedure does not 'spend' any alpha associated with the test of the null hypothesis.
31|The Independent Data Safety Monitoring Committee (IDSMC) may recommend altering aspects of
32|the study (e.g. early termination on futility grounds) if the CP is unacceptably low. A CP <20% is
33|suggested in the protocol as a guide for the IDSMC for defining 'an unacceptably low CP'. Refer to
34|interim analysis section of the protocol for additional information on feasibility and safety
35|monitoring overseen by the IDSMC.

9|Overall Survival (OS) - Primary Analysis of Primary Endpoint
10|Overall survival (OS) time for each treatment group will be quantified using the Kaplan-Meier
11|method and compared using an unstratified log-rank test. An unadjusted Cox PH model will be used
12|to estimate the hazard ratio (with 95% CI). In addition, if early stopping is triggered by rejection of
13|the null hypothesis at an interim analysis (see Section 4), the conditional mean-adjusted estimator
14|will be used to obtain an estimate of hazard ratio for OS corrected for early stopping and a 95%
15|confidence interval for the estimate will be obtained using bootstrapping3. This will be presented
16|along with the conventional HR and confidence interval for reference purposes. Section 4 and 9
17|provide detail on the interim, adjusted, and subgroup analyses that are planned to be conducted on
18|OS.

21|PSA Progression Free Survival time for each treatment group will be quantified using the Kaplan-
22|Meier method and compared using an unstratified log-rank test. An unadjusted Cox PH model will be
23|used to estimate the hazard ratio (with 95% CI). Section 9 provide detail on the subgroup analyses
24|that are planned to be conducted on PSA PSF.
25|8.7

28|for PSA PFS. Section 9 provide detail on the subgroup analyses that are planned to be conducted on

30|8.8
31|Safety Data Analysis
32|Adverse Events (AEs) and Serious Adverse Events (SAEs) will be tabulated by treatment received (see
33|Section 3) and CTCAE criteria including system organ class, term, and (worst) grade.
34|8.9
35|Quality of life (QoL)
36|The QoL analyses will comprise a primary and a secondary set of approaches (next described).
37|
38|8.9.1
39|Primary Approach: Deterioration-Free Survival
40|A deterioration-free survival (DetFS) endpoint will be constructed as a marker of overall net-benefit
41|over the on-treatment period. This is defined as the time from randomisation to the first of the
42|following events: a 10-point or more deterioration in health status from baseline (without
43|subsequent 10-point or more improvement compared with baseline), clinical progression, death, or
44|treatment discontinuation. If a patient experiences none of these events, they will be censored. The
45|censoring date will be the latest of the following: the date of the patient's last QoL assessment; the
46|date of the patient's last assessment during the 'on treatment' phase where clinical progression
47|status is recorded as 'no'; and, the maximum date the patient is last known not to have progressed
48|collected during the 'post-treatment follow-up' phase. Two DFS endpoints will be derived using
49|different markers of health status deterioration based on the EORTC QLQ-C30: one used the Physical
50|
51|3 Shimura M. Comparison of conditional bias-adjusted estimators for interim analysis in clinical trials
52|with survival data. Statistics in medicine 2017;36(13):2067

1|
2|Page 10
3|
4|Function Scale (DetFSPF), and the other used the General Health Scale (DetFSGHS). The treatment
5|groups will be compared on DetFSPF and DFSGHS using an unstratified log-rank test. Kaplan-Meier
6|curves will be prepared and used to estimate median DetFS with 95% confidence intervals. An
7|estimate of the hazard ratio for the treatment effect will be obtained using a Cox proportional
8|hazard regression model without stratification factors.
9|
10|8.9.2
11|Secondary Approach: Mixed Model for Repeated Measures
12|Scale scores from the QLQ-C30, PR25 and EQ5D will be summarised by treatment group over time,
13|and are planned to be analysed using a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM). The MMRM
14|will include covariates for baseline, treatment arm, post-baseline time-point, and a treatment-by-
15|time point interaction. A blinded analysis (of interim) QoL data will be used to refine the analysis
16|method. This will include: (i) specifying the covariance structure after evaluation of various options
17|(including compound symmetry and autoregressive) using the AIC statistic; and (ii) specifying the
18|strategy for accommodating any highly skewed data (e.g. log transformation, or split at median or
19|other logical value with analysis of the resultant categorical endpoint performed using a repeated
20|measures generalised linear model with a logit link function).
21|8.10 Quality-Adjusted Survival (QAS)
22|Within-trial estimates of quality-adjusted survival (QAS) will be calculated for each randomised
23|treatment group4. This will involve combining the QoL utility function estimated from the repeated
24|measures analysis of the EQ-5D collected up to treatment cessation with the time-to-treatment-
25|cessation function estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method; and, combining post treatment
26|cessation QoL estimate(s) (from external sources) with the survival-post-treatment-cessation
27|function estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. The QAS estimates will be truncated at the time
28|point when either of the arms has <10% of patients at risk5. Confidence intervals will be constructed
29|using bootstrapping. The applicability of approaches for deriving utilities from the EORTC QLQ-C30,
30|to use as an alternative to the EQ-5D, may also be explored in sensitivity analyses.
31|8.11 Analysis of Health Outcomes Relative to Costs
32|Australian unit costs will be applied to the resource usage data (See Section 2.6) to estimate the
33|within-trial cost difference (in Australian dollars) between randomised arms. A within-trial estimate
34|of the incremental cost-effectiveness of the addition of enzalutamide to standard treatment will be
35|calculated in terms of the cost difference relative to the quality-adjusted survival (QAS) difference.
36|
37|The feasibility of extrapolating beyond the within-trial estimate of cost-effectiveness using modelling
38|methods will be explored.

41|(See Section 6) will be investigated for the ITT population. A comparison between randomised

questions.wording: Were the data that produced this result analysed in accordance with a pre-specified analysis plan that was finalized before unblinded outcome data were available for analysis?
questions.official_guidance: To avoid the possibility of selection of the reported result, finalization of the analysis intentions must precede availability of unblinded outcome data to the trial investigators. Changes to analysis plans that were made before unblinded outcome data were available, or that were clearly unrelated to the results, do not raise concerns about bias in selection of the reported result.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 63, Box 11, signalling question 5.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether data producing this result followed a pre-specified plan finalized before unblinded outcome data were available.
questions.decision_rule: Compare the approved Result with the applicable plan for the exact intervention comparison, cohort, endpoint, time window, population, analysis, and effect measure. Distinguish source creation/version and amendment dates from trial events and retrieval time; only compare chronology when the relevant events and precision are established. Changes made before unblinded data were available, or clearly unrelated to results such as a broken machine, do not raise concerns.
evidence_needed: A sufficiently detailed protocol or SAP, its source-located chronology and finalization date relative to unblinded outcome data, and the reported analysis.

For an original plan and an amended plan, capture the source-located content and chronology separately. An embedded SAP can be applicable evidence when its comparison, cohort, and Result fields match; an absent or unresolved plan remains an information limit.
questions.no_information_rule: Use a definitive answer when firm evidence establishes timing and correspondence. Use a probable answer when source facts and trial circumstances support only an inference. Use no_information when neither is supported. A plan mention or matching endpoint alone does not establish timing.

answer_anchors.text: The result follows a sufficiently detailed plan finalized before unblinded outcome data were available.
The result did not follow such a pre-specified plan.
Analysis intentions or their timing are not sufficiently reported.

considerations: Assess correspondence between the applicable plan and the exact approved Result: outcome, time point, population, effect measure, and analysis must be compared.

Assess applicability before chronology: a platform or master plan may cover several comparisons and cohorts, so its presence does not establish applicability to the approved Result. Establish chronology separately: plan finalization must precede availability of unblinded outcome data; a source creation date, registry posting or update date, amendment date, or retrieval date is not automatically the relevant trial chronology.

Current registry content does not establish unseen historical intent, and a data cutoff is not investigator unblinding. Preserve unresolved applicability or chronology instead of filling the gap from report wording that merely looks prespecified.

Results-driven selection is a separate concern from whether a plan exists or whether its chronology is known. Do not infer selection merely from an amendment or from a mismatch without evidence that the choice was driven by results.

Neutral paired control: an applicable plan for the approved cohort differs from a platform plan for another phase; pre-unblinding finalization differs from ambiguous chronology only in the timing premise.
invalid_shortcuts: a protocol mention without date or detail
current registry content treated as historical intent
a data cutoff treated as investigator unblinding
a platform master plan treated as applicable to every comparison

evidence.transcription: Supplementary Figure S1, CONSORT diagram: 1125 men with metastatic prostate cancer commencing androgen deprivation therapy were randomized. Enzalutamide: allocated 563; received allocated intervention 563; did not receive 0; lost to follow-up 0; withdrew consent for follow-up 4; analyzed as ITT 563; excluded from safety analysis 0. NSAA: allocated 562; received allocated intervention 558; did not receive 4; lost to follow-up 2; withdrew consent for follow-up 8; analyzed as ITT 562; 4 who received no study drug were excluded from safety and treatment exposure analyses. Footnote a: median survival follow-up for the 4 enzalutamide participants who withdrew consent was 7.2 months (IQR 2.0 to 24.4). Footnote b: median survival follow-up for the 10 NSAA participants who withdrew consent or were lost to follow-up was 7.7 months (IQR 0.4 to 12.0); 2 withdrew consent immediately after randomization.

Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer

Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

n engl j med 381;2 nejm.org July 11, 2019
125
Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
The baseline characteristics of all the patients
are summarized in Table 1 and detailed in the
Supplementary Appendix. High-volume disease
was present in 52% of the patients in the two
groups. Early docetaxel treatment was planned
in 45% of the patients (including in 61% of those
with high-volume disease and in 27% of those
with low-volume disease) but was not adminis-
tered to 22 patients, 11 in each of the randomly
assigned treatment groups. The full planned
course of six cycles of docetaxel was given to 159
of 243 patients (65%) in the enzalutamide group
and 181 of 238 (76%) in the standard-care group.
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis of the primary end
point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
independent data and safety monitoring com-
mittee recommended that the unblinded results
be provided to the trial executive committee so
that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
The results that are reported here include 10
additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
view to ascertain the survival status of all the
patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
follow-up of 34 months.
At the time of this analysis, there were 102
deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
fected by adjustments for geographical region,
volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
conditions. The median survival time was not yet
estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier
estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80%
(based on 94 events) in the enzalutamide group
and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-
care group.
Progression-free Survival
The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
free survival and clinical progression-free survival
were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
the between-group difference in PSA progres-
sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
survival remained highly significant after adjust-
ment for multiple comparisons.
Subgroup Analyses
The effects of enzalutamide on overall survival
were smaller among the patients in the stratified
subgroups with respect to bone antiresorptive
therapy, planned early docetaxel treatment, and
high-volume disease (Fig. 2, and Table S3 in the
Supplementary Appendix). After adjustment for
multiple comparisons, P values for heterogeneity
of the treatment effect of enzalutamide were
0.14 for volume of disease, 0.14 for early docetax-
el treatment, and 0.06 for the use of bone anti-
resorptive therapy.
We anticipated that the smaller number of
deaths would limit the reliability of subgroup
analyses of overall survival. Thus, we specified
in the analysis plan that subgroup analyses of
progression-free survival would also be per-
formed to take advantage of the larger number
of events for this secondary end point. The ef-
fects of enzalutamide on clinical progression-
free survival were noted in all predefined sub-
groups, including those with early docetaxel
treatment (Fig. 3, and Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix). The analyses of treatment effects
on clinical progression-free survival according to
the volume of disease and planned early docetax-
el treatment showed consistently smaller effects
of enzalutamide in patients with high-volume
disease and in those with early docetaxel treat-
ment. However, P values for heterogeneity of the
treatment effect of enzalutamide were no longer
significant after adjustment for multiple com-
parisons (Figs. S2, S3, and S4 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix).
Subsequent Anticancer Therapies
Treatment after progression was initiated at the
discretion of the patients and their physicians.

2|1 Introduction
3|The aim of the ENZAMET trial is to determine the effectiveness of enzalutamide versus conventional
4|non-steroidal anti-androgen (NSAA) in men with metastatic prostate cancer.
5|
6|The study is an open label phase III trial that randomises eligible patients to receive, until disease
7|progression or prohibitive toxicity, either: oral enzalutamide 160mg daily or conventional oral NSAA
8|treatment. All participants are treated with surgical castration or a Luteinizing Hormone-Releasing
9|Hormone Analog (LHRHA)
10|
11|The randomisation is performed in a 1:1 ratio and is stratified by volume of disease (high volume yes
12|versus no), use of early docetaxel (yes versus no), antiresorptive therapy (yes versus no),
13|comorbidities (Adult Co-morbidity Evaluation ACE-27 score: 0-1 vs 2-3), and treating institution
14|(Study Site).
15|
16|The target population is men with metastatic prostate cancer commencing androgen deprivation
17|therapy. Key eligibility criteria include metastatic prostate cancer, adequate organ function and
18|ECOG performance status 0-2.
19|
20|The primary objective is to determine the effect of enzalutamide on overall survival (OS). The
21|secondary objectives are to determine the effect of enzalutamide on: prostate specific antigen
22|progression free survival (PCGW2), clinical progression free survival (imaging, symptoms, signs),
23|adverse events (CTCAE v4.03), health related quality of life (EORTC QLQ C-30, PR-25 and EQ-5D-5L),
24|and health outcomes relative to costs.
25|
26|Correlative objectives include: to identify biomarkers that are prognostic and/or predictive of
27|response to treatment, safety and resistance to study treatment. A separate analysis plan will be
28|prepared to address these objectives.
29|
30|The statisticians working on this study are aware of the importance treating any unblinded efficacy
31|results as highly sensitive and taking reasonable measures to keep such information confidential,
32|despite this being an open label study. DRAFT tabulations/analyses of efficacy endpoints should be
33|prepared using dummy treatment allocations, or be pooled across randomised groups. Occasions
34|where tabulations/analyses of efficacy endpoints are prepared by actual treatment allocation (for an
35|interim analysis and/or the final analysis) will be documented. Access to the analysis programming
36|environment will be restricted to authorised personnel.
37|2 Endpoint Derivation
38|
39|A central clinical review will be performed on the results of the endpoint derivations specified
40|below. A series of specific programmed endpoint checks are also performed, with any issues being
41|centrally reviewed. Treatment allocation will not be included on the review outputs. Any instances
42|Page 4
43|

1|

3|endorsed by the Clinical Lead (on behalf of the TMC) and documented in the study report.
4|2.1
5|Overall Survival (OS) (Primary Endpoint)
6|Overall survival is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to date of death from any
7|cause, or the date last known alive (at which point the observation is censored).
8|2.2
9|PSA Progression Free Survival (PSA PFS)
10|PSA progression free survival (PSA PFS) is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to
11|the date of first evidence of PSA progression, clinical progression, or death from any cause,
12|whichever occurs first, or the date of last known follow-up without PSA progression (at which point
13|the observation is censored).
14|2.3
15|Clinical Progression Free Survival (Clinical PFS)
16|Clinical progression free survival is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to the
17|date of first clinical evidence of disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurs first,
18|or the date of last known follow-up without clinical progression (at which point the observation is
19|censored). Clinical progression is defined by progression on imaging, development of symptoms
20|attributable to cancer progression, or initiation of other anticancer treatment for prostate cancer.
21|2.4
22|Safety
23|The NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events Version 4.0 (NCI CTCAE) will be used to
24|classify and grade the intensity of adverse events whilst on treatment, at progression, and 30-42
25|days after the last dose of study treatment.
26|2.5
27|Quality of Life (QoL)
28|The core EORTC QoL Questionnaire (QLQ-C30) will be used in conjunction with the disease specific
29|module for prostate cancer (PR25). The EQ-5D will be used to obtain utility valuations on the health
30|states experienced by participants. All instruments will be scored according to standard conventions
31|(see Section 10.1 and 10.2).
32|2.6
33|Health Care Resource Usage
34|Information on the following areas of health-care resource usage will be collected: protocol therapy
35|and hospitalisations (for all participants by trial staff via standard case record forms (CRFs), visits to
36|health professionals (for Australian participants via Medicare benefits scheme (MBS) and for other
37|regions as specified separately in their Group Specific Appendix (GSA), and non-protocol medications
38|(for Australian participants via Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) and for other regions as
39|separately specified in their GSA).
40|3 Analysis Sets
41|The intention-to-treat (ITT) population will comprise all randomised participants. The per-protocol
42|population will comprise all randomised participants that are deemed eligible/evaluable on blinded
43|central clinical review. The safety population will comprise all randomised participants that are
44|deemed eligible/evaluable on blinded central clinical review who received at least one

2|Page 4
3|
4|1 Introduction
5|The aim of the ENZAMET trial is to determine the effectiveness of enzalutamide versus conventional
6|non-steroidal anti-androgen (NSAA) in men with metastatic prostate cancer.
7|
8|The study is an open label phase III trial that randomises eligible patients to receive, until disease
9|progression or prohibitive toxicity, either: oral enzalutamide 160mg daily or conventional oral NSAA
10|treatment. All participants are treated with surgical castration or a Luteinizing Hormone-Releasing
11|Hormone Analog (LHRHA)
12|
13|The randomisation is performed in a 1:1 ratio and is stratified by volume of disease (high volume yes
14|versus no), use of early docetaxel (yes versus no), antiresorptive therapy (yes versus no),
15|comorbidities (Adult Co-morbidity Evaluation ACE-27 score: 0-1 vs 2-3), and treating institution
16|(Study Site).
17|
18|The target population is men with metastatic prostate cancer commencing androgen deprivation
19|therapy. Key eligibility criteria include metastatic prostate cancer, adequate organ function and
20|ECOG performance status 0-2.
21|
22|The primary objective is to determine the effect of enzalutamide on overall survival (OS). The
23|secondary objectives are to determine the effect of enzalutamide on: prostate specific antigen
24|progression free survival (PCGW2), clinical progression free survival (imaging, symptoms, signs),
25|adverse events (CTCAE v4.03), health related quality of life (EORTC QLQ C-30, PR-25 and EQ-5D-5L),
26|and health outcomes relative to costs.
27|
28|Correlative objectives include: to identify biomarkers that are prognostic and/or predictive of
29|response to treatment, safety and resistance to study treatment. A separate analysis plan will be
30|prepared to address these objectives.
31|
32|The statisticians working on this study are aware of the importance treating any unblinded efficacy
33|results as highly sensitive and taking reasonable measures to keep such information confidential,
34|despite this being an open label study. DRAFT tabulations/analyses of efficacy endpoints should be
35|prepared using dummy treatment allocations, or be pooled across randomised groups. Occasions
36|where tabulations/analyses of efficacy endpoints are prepared by actual treatment allocation (for an
37|interim analysis and/or the final analysis) will be documented. Access to the analysis programming
38|environment will be restricted to authorised personnel.
39|2 Endpoint Derivation
40|A central clinical review will be performed on the results of the endpoint derivations specified
41|below. A series of specific programmed endpoint checks are also performed, with any issues being
42|centrally reviewed. Treatment allocation will not be included on the review outputs. Any instances
43|where the specifications below are overruled on the basis of the clinical review findings will be
44|endorsed by the Clinical Lead (on behalf of the TMC) and documented in the study report.

1|
2|
3|
4|Page 5
5|
6|2.1
7|Overall Survival (OS) (Primary Endpoint)
8|Overall survival is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to date of death from any
9|cause, or the date last known alive (at which point the observation is censored).
10|2.2
11|PSA Progression Free Survival (PSA PFS)
12|PSA progression free survival (PSA PFS) is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to
13|the date of first evidence of PSA progression, clinical progression, or death from any cause,
14|whichever occurs first, or the date of last PSA test without PSA progression (at which point the
15|observation is censored).
16|2.3
17|Clinical Progression Free Survival (Clinical PFS)
18|Clinical progression free survival is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to the
19|date of first clinical evidence of disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurs first,
20|or the date of last known follow-up without clinical progression (at which point the observation is
21|censored). The censoring date will be the latest of the following: the date of the patient's last
22|assessment during the 'on treatment' phase where clinical progression status is recorded as 'no';
23|and, the maximum date the patient is last known not to have progressed collected during the 'post-
24|treatment follow-up' phase. Clinical progression is defined by progression on imaging, development
25|of symptoms attributable to cancer progression, or initiation of other anticancer treatment for
26|prostate cancer.
27|2.4
28|Safety
29|The NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events Version 4.03 (NCI CTCAE) will be used to
30|classify and grade the intensity of adverse events whilst on treatment, at progression, and 30-42
31|days after the last dose of study treatment.
32|2.5
33|Quality of Life (QoL)
34|The core EORTC QoL Questionnaire (QLQ-C30) will be used in conjunction with the disease specific
35|module for prostate cancer (PR25). The EQ-5D will be used to obtain utility valuations on the health
36|states experienced by participants. All instruments will be scored according to standard conventions
37|(see Section 10.1 and 10.2).
38|2.6
39|Health Care Resource Usage
40|Information on the following areas of health-care resource usage will be collected: protocol therapy
41|and hospitalisations (for all participants by trial staff via standard case record forms (CRFs), visits to
42|health professionals (for Australian participants via Medicare benefits scheme (MBS) and for other
43|regions as specified separately in their Group Specific Appendix (GSA), and non-protocol medications
44|(for Australian participants via Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) and for other regions as
45|separately specified in their GSA).
46|3 Analysis Sets
47|All randomised participants will be eligible for inclusion in the full analysis set in accordance with the
48|intention-to-treat analysis principle. The full analysis set thus comprises the intention-to-treat (ITT)
49|population. The per-protocol population will comprise all randomised participants that are deemed
50|eligible/evaluable on blinded central clinical review. Patients are classified according to study

3|Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
4|coexisting conditions rated as 0 [none] or 1 [mild]
5|vs. 2 [moderate] or 3 [severe or multiple condi-
6|tions]), and trial site.
7|Trial Oversight
8|The trial was led by the Australian and New
9|Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
10|Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
11|Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
12|Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
13|sponsorship and coordination was performed by
14|Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
15|Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
16|Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
17|in the United States. The trial was designed by the
18|ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
19|analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
20|The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
21|ing of the manuscript.
22|Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
23|financial support for trial conduct; representa-
24|tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
25|tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
26|volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
27|accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
28|Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
29|drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
30|were accessed according to local standard prac-
31|tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
32|completeness of the reported data and for the
33|fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
34|An independent data and safety monitoring
35|committee reviewed the progress and results of
36|the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
37|with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
38|guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
39|protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
40|proved as required at each participating institu-
41|tion. All the patients provided written informed
42|consent.
43|End Points
44|The primary end point of overall survival was
45|measured as the interval from randomization to
46|death from any cause or to the date at which the
47|patient was last known to be alive. The second-
48|ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
49|was measured as the interval from randomiza-
50|tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
51|cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
52|Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
53|in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
54|and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
55|sion, death from any cause, or the last known
56|date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
57|secondary end point of clinical progression was
58|defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
59|gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
60|Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
61|the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
62|mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
63|development of symptoms attributable to cancer
64|progression; or the initiation of another antican-
65|cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
66|means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
67|mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
68|gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
69|images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
70|verse events were graded according to the Na-
71|tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
72|Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
73|verse-event data were collected during the treat-
74|ment period, with a final safety assessment
75|performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
76|the trial regimen.
77|Statistical Analysis
78|We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
79|tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
80|of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
81|death in the enzalutamide group than in the
82|standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
83|two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
84|culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
85|65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
86|two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
87|with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
88|cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
89|an interim analysis of overall survival after the
90|occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
91|deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
92|spending function. Protocol version 3, which
93|was written after external evidence became
94|available for improved overall survival with early
95|abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
96|of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
97|and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
98|trial executive committee made these decisions
99|without any knowledge of outcomes in each
100|treatment group.
101|The New England Journal of Medicine is produced by NEJM Group, a division of the Massachusetts Medical Society.

1|n engl j med 381;2 nejm.org July 11, 2019
2|125
3|Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
4|The baseline characteristics of all the patients
5|are summarized in Table 1 and detailed in the
6|Supplementary Appendix. High-volume disease
7|was present in 52% of the patients in the two
8|groups. Early docetaxel treatment was planned
9|in 45% of the patients (including in 61% of those
10|with high-volume disease and in 27% of those
11|with low-volume disease) but was not adminis-
12|tered to 22 patients, 11 in each of the randomly
13|assigned treatment groups. The full planned
14|course of six cycles of docetaxel was given to 159
15|of 243 patients (65%) in the enzalutamide group
16|and 181 of 238 (76%) in the standard-care group.
17|Overall Survival
18|The first interim analysis of the primary end
19|point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
20|occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
21|independent data and safety monitoring com-
22|mittee recommended that the unblinded results
23|be provided to the trial executive committee so
24|that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
25|mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
26|rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
27|esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
28|The results that are reported here include 10
29|additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
30|view to ascertain the survival status of all the
31|patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
32|follow-up of 34 months.
33|At the time of this analysis, there were 102
34|deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
35|in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
36|death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
37|0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
38|fected by adjustments for geographical region,
39|volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
40|ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
41|conditions. The median survival time was not yet
42|estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier

The first interim analysis of the primary end
point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
independent data and safety monitoring com-
mittee recommended that the unblinded results

mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
esis that was specified for this interim analysis.

additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-

patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median

answers.justification: The applicable SAP is explicitly for ENZAMET and version 2.0 is dated 10 February 2019. It defines PSA PFS from randomization and prespecifies Kaplan-Meier, unstratified log-rank, and an unadjusted Cox model for the HR with 95% CI, matching the approved all-randomized PSA-PFS HR. The main report says unblinded interim results were recommended for provision to the trial executive committee on 7 March 2019, after the SAP version date; it also describes the executive committee's protocol-version decisions as made without knowledge of treatment-group outcomes. This supports, but does not prove, that the final analysis intentions preceded investigator access to unblinded results.
unknowns: The SAP approval signature and date fields are blank, so the 10 February version date is the available finalization chronology.
The report describes the DSMC recommendation to provide unblinded results on 7 March, but does not separately state the first date any trial investigator or statistician obtained unblinded data.

counterevidence.implication: The printed version date supports chronology but is not a completed approval signature date; this limits certainty and supports a probable rather than definitive answer.

answers.justification: The SAP gives one PSA-PFS definition and censoring rule; the main report's PCWG2-based PSA-PFS definition matches the requested measure. It separately defines clinical PFS, and the article reports its estimate alongside PSA PFS. Thus the distinct PFS endpoint was not selectively omitted. No alternative PSA-PFS scales or scheduled measurements are identified in these passages.
unknowns: The SAP version-change summary says censoring details for PSA PFS were added, and the final SAP operationalizes censoring at the last PSA test while the report says last known follow-up without PSA progression; the sources do not explain this wording difference.

answers.justification: For the overall PSA-PFS comparison, the SAP prespecifies an unstratified log-rank test and unadjusted Cox HR with 95% CI, which matches the reported HR. The report also presents clinical PFS and planned subgroup findings; those are distinct outcomes or subgroup questions, not competing estimates for the approved all-randomized overall PSA-PFS result. The SAP's adjusted Cox strategy is specified for OS; PSA-PFS subgroup analyses are separately planned. There is no indication that the reported overall PSA-PFS model was selected from competing eligible analyses based on its results.
unknowns: The sources do not describe every analysis actually run, but they identify the primary overall PSA-PFS method and distinguish the planned adjusted and subgroup analyses.

Eligible patients were randomly assigned in a
1:1 ratio to receive enzalutamide (at a dose of
160 mg daily) or a standard nonsteroidal antian-
drogen drug (bicalutamide, nilutamide, or flu-
tamide) (standard-care group) until the occur-
rence of clinical disease progression or prohibitive
toxic effects. In the two groups, background ther-
apy included continuous testosterone suppression.
After the enrollment of 88 patients (mainly from
Australia and New Zealand), the early adminis-
tration of docetaxel with testosterone suppression
was permitted in protocol version 2 (as revised on
November 2014) as a stratification factor before
randomization, according to evidence showing
improved survival with this approach.1 The deci-
sion to initiate early treatment with docetaxel was
left up to the individual patients and their physi-
cians. If docetaxel was administered, the regimen
consisted of 75 mg per square meter of body-
surface area, without prednisone or prednisolone,
given every 3 weeks for a maximum of six cycles.
Up to two cycles of docetaxel were permitted be-
fore randomization.
The central randomization system implement-
ed minimization with a random component. Ran-
domization was stratified according to the volume
of disease (high [defined as the presence of vis-
ceral metastases or at least four bone lesions with
at least one lesion located beyond the vertebral
bodies and pelvis] or low), planned use of early
docetaxel (yes or no), planned use of bone anti-
resorptive therapy (yes or no), the score on the
Adult Comorbidity Evaluation 27 (ACE-27)17 (with

Prior to randomization, treating clinicians and participants must decide if early treatment with
docetaxel is to be undertaken. Randomisation will be performed via a central randomization
system that stratifies for volume of disease (high versus low), site, co-morbidities (ACE-27 0-1
versus 2-3), use of anti-resorptive therapy (denosumab, zoledronic acid or neither) at time of
starting ADT, and planned use of docetaxel. The decisions regarding use of early docetaxel or of
anti-resorptive therapy, must be made and documented prior to randomization.

Participants will be randomly allocated (1:1) to receive either enzalutamide OR NSAA in addition to
their LHRHA (or surgical castration). Study treatment should be planned to start within 7 days after
randomisation.

The instructions for the randomisation system provided in the Study Manual should be followed.
Confirmation of each randomisation will be provided to the site.

METHODS
In this open-label, randomized, phase 3 trial, we assigned patients to receive tes-
tosterone suppression plus either open-label enzalutamide or a standard nonsteroidal
antiandrogen therapy (standard-care group). The primary end point was overall
survival. Secondary end points included progression-free survival as determined by
the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level, clinical progression-free survival, and
adverse events.

The first interim analysis of the primary end
point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
independent data and safety monitoring com-
mittee recommended that the unblinded results
be provided to the trial executive committee so
that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
The results that are reported here include 10
additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
view to ascertain the survival status of all the
patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
follow-up of 34 months.

8.6
PSA Progression Free Survival (PSA PFS)
PSA Progression Free Survival time for each treatment group will be quantified using the Kaplan-
Meier method and compared using an unstratified log-rank test. An unadjusted Cox PH model will be
used to estimate the hazard ratio (with 95% CI). Section 9 provide detail on the subgroup analyses
that are planned to be conducted on PSA PSF.
8.7
Clinical Progression Free Survival (Clinical PFS)
Clinical Progression Free Survival will be analysed using the same approach as that described above
for PSA PFS. Section 9 provide detail on the subgroup analyses that are planned to be conducted on
clinical PSF

2.2
PSA Progression Free Survival (PSA PFS)
PSA progression free survival (PSA PFS) is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to
the date of first evidence of PSA progression, clinical progression, or death from any cause,
whichever occurs first, or the date of last PSA test without PSA progression (at which point the
observation is censored).

The primary end point of overall survival was

Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the

65% in the standard-care group on the basis of

with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate

Progression-free Survival
The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
free survival and clinical progression-free survival
were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
the between-group difference in PSA progres-
sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
survival remained highly significant after adjust-
ment for multiple comparisons.

facts.text:
8.6
PSA Progression Free Survival (PSA PFS)
PSA Progression Free Survival time for each treatment group will be quantified using the Kaplan-
Meier method and compared using an unstratified log-rank test. An unadjusted Cox PH model will be
used to estimate the hazard ratio (with 95% CI). Section 9 provide detail on the subgroup analyses
that are planned to be conducted on PSA PSF.
8.7
Clinical Progression Free Survival (Clinical PFS)
Clinical Progression Free Survival will be analysed using the same approach as that described above
for PSA PFS. Section 9 provide detail on the subgroup analyses that are planned to be conducted on
clinical PSF

Progression-free Survival
The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
free survival and clinical progression-free survival
were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
the between-group difference in PSA progres-
sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
survival remained highly significant after adjust-
ment for multiple comparisons.

Page 11

groups will be undertaken using a stratified long-rank test. An adjusted hazard ratio (with 95% CI)
will be obtained from a Cox PH model that includes the stratification factors as covariates. These
analyses will be performed on the ITT population.

The consistency of the treatment effect on OS across the stratification factors and other pre-
specified baseline characteristics (See Section 0) will be tested by fitting the relevant factor-by-
treatment interaction term in a Cox regression model along with the associated main effects terms.
The subgroup analyses will be repeated using PSA PFS and clinical PFS as the endpoints.

A clinical question of particular importance and interest is whether early docetaxel modifies the
effect of enzalutamide in patients with high volume disease. The corresponding analysis will involve
fitting a docetaxel-by-treatment interaction term, along with the associated main effects terms, in a
Cox regression model applied to PSA PFS in the cohort of patients with high volume disease in the
ITT population. Because that analysis will only include high disease volume patient, it will have less
statistical power to detect effect modification than those subgroup analyses applied to the full ITT
population. Note that exposure to docetaxel is not randomised.

The hypothesis tests from the planned adjusted and subgroup analysis described above will be
considered within the following discrete families: (1) a set of adjusted analyses on OS; (2) a set of
subgroup analyses on OS; (3) a set of subgroup analyses on PSA PFS; and (4) a set of subgroup
analyses on clinical PFS. Due consideration will be given to the family-wise type I error rate when
conservatively interpreting the p-values within each of family of tests, and the Benjamini-Hochberg
procedure6 will be used to calculate adjusted p-values with the family-wise type I error being set to
5%.





6 Huque M. F. Validity of the Hochberg procedure revisited for clinical trial applications. Stat Med
2016;35:5-20

ENZAMET’s RoB 2 assessment is finalized. Overall risk of bias is **Some concerns**, driven by outcome measurement; the other four domains are Low.

| Domain | Judgment |
|---|---|
| Randomization | Low |
| Deviations from intended interventions | Low |
| Missing outcome data | Low |
| Outcome measurement | Some concerns |
| Selection of the reported result | Low |

For selection, the final SAP is dated 10 February 2019 and specifies the PSA-PFS analysis used. The report says unblinded interim results were recommended for provision to the trial executive committee on 7 March. I rated this domain Low, while noting that the SAP’s approval signature is blank and its censoring wording differs slightly from the report.

The full article reports HR **0.39** (95% CI **0.33–0.47**, P<0.001); the abstract’s omission of the confidence interval does not change the assessed result.
